summaries.summary: Chatbots have evolved from AIML, handcrafted rules, and information retrieval to neural conversation models and KB-grounded systems, but existing systems do not learn new knowledge during conversation.
KB completion is binary classification over query triples, but existing approaches assume known entities and relations, preventing new knowledge with unknown entities or relations in conversations.
The paper removes the KBC closed-world assumption, defines open-world knowledge base completion (OKBC), and formulates conversational knowledge learning and inference as interactive OKBC.
Conversation utterances yield true facts and queries; true facts are incorporated into the KB, while query facts require OKBC when “Obama,” “BornIn,” or “USA” is unknown.
OKBC is the core of a conversational knowledge learning engine, and the paper assumes fact/relation extraction, resolution, and related-fact guessing are handled by other sub-systems.

LiLi mimics human interactive knowledge acquisition and reasoning through processing and interactive actions, retaining acquired facts and using accumulated knowledge to guide future interaction and learning.
This setting is ideal for NLP applications like dialog and question-answering systems that allow human interaction and require real-time inference.
LiLi extends closed-world path-ranking and C-PR to OKBC, using bidirectional random walks, source-target context, and an extended compositional vector space model with continual learning.
LiLi dynamically formulates questions, uses acquired supporting facts for inference, applies RL for strategy and prediction, and is evaluated on Freebase and WordNet.
The authors know of no knowledge learning system that learns new knowledge during conversation, so the section discusses other related work.

Existing KB completion, NELL, interactive language learning, question-asking, and dialogue systems differ from LiLi by lacking open-world handling, interactive knowledge learning, query-specific strategies, or lifelong prediction-model training.
General lifelong learning methods learn only one task type and are unsuitable for LiLi’s interleaving of RL, supervised, and interactive learning.

LiLi combines an RL model for query-specific OKBC inference strategies with a lifelong prediction model, improving through user interaction and knowledge retention while addressing three OKBC challenges.
LiLi maps open-world to closed-world by asking users for clues for unknown relations or connecting link queries (CLQs) for unknown entities, reducing OKBC to KBC.
To address KB sparseness, LiLi uses “@-?-@” as a missing link marker, extracts complete and incomplete paths, and asks missing link queries (MLQs) for path completion.
If users cannot respond to MLQs or CLQs, LiLi uses a guessing mechanism to fill the gap and continue inference.
LiLi’s Knowledge Store (KS) contains a Knowledge Graph, Relation-Entity Matrix, Task Experience Store using Matthews correlation coefficient (MCC), and Incomplete Feature DB for MLQs.

The RL model updates on unseen states, KS is continuously updated, and the prediction model transfers parameters from similar past tasks while using MCC-based experience to improve poorly learned tasks.
LiLi uses an Inference Stack to hold query and RL state information, processing user clues first so prediction models are learned before inference and OKBC becomes KBC.
An OKBC query is represented as a data instance containing the query triple, interaction limit, MDP transition history, mode, and feature set, then initialized for RL strategy formulation.
Strategy formulation is an inference game where LiLi wins if the relation becomes known and path features are extracted, enabling prediction-model training and inference.
LiLi models strategy formulation as an MDP with 10 binary state variables and 6 actions, using Q-learning with an ε-greedy strategy and rewards for valid actions.
When unseen states cause repeated invalid actions, LiLi switches to training mode and randomly explores actions to learn the optimal action through fault-tolerant learning.

During action execution, LiLi updates stack-top state and experience for invalid actions, while valid actions set the next state, perform operations, monitor interaction limits, and decrement limits for user queries.
LiLi selects incomplete paths for MLQs using frequency and contextual similarity, and guesses missing links using thresholds over [-1, 1] when users do not respond.
LiLi asks CLQs for unknown entities by selecting the most contextually relevant node using contextual relevance computed with word embedding.
LiLi extracts path features, updates incomplete features, trains prediction models with complete features, and monitors requirements to control MLQ interactions.

Lifelong relation prediction trains relation-specific models using 10% of instances, LSTM-composed features, cosine similarity, log-likelihood, MCC updates, inverse models, and relation-specific prediction thresholds.
LiLi transfers weights from the most similar past task using truncated SVD of the Relation-Entity Matrix, randomly initializing weights when no suitable source relation exists.
A Figure 1 example shows LiLi acquiring a “CitizenOf” clue, connecting “Obama,” enumerating paths between “Obama” and “USA,” filling a missing link, and making inference.
The experiments evaluate LiLi’s predictive performance and strategy formulation abilities.
The evaluation uses Freebase FB15k and WordNet, building large original KB graphs augmented with inverse triples following existing KBC methods.
A simulated user is created for each KB, with labeled datasets, simulated user knowledge bases, and base KBs derived from the original KB.
For Freebase, 86 relations were found, 50 selected, 25% made unknown, 1000 triples split into 60% training, 10% validation and 20% test, while WordNet uses all 18 relations.
Because no existing KBC method solves OKBC, various versions of LiLi are used as baselines.
BG fills missing or connecting links with “@-RelatedTo-@” blindly when the user does not respond, without a guessing mechanism.
w/o PTS removes LiLi’s requests for additional clues via past task selection for skillset improvement.
Strategy formulation is evaluated by Coverage, while predictive performance uses Avg. MCC and avg. +ve F1 score.
Table 5 shows Coverage dropping to 0.47 without interaction, rising to 0.97 with one interaction and 1 with more, while Table 6 shows LiLi outperforming baselines.
More clues significantly improve LiLi, while user responses to MLQs and CLQs help modestly; guessing and continual learning yield avg. +ve F1 of 0.57 and 0.62 on FB and WN.
The paper formulates continuous conversational knowledge learning as OKBC, proposes LiLi using RL and lifelong interaction, and reports effectiveness in predictive quality and strategy formulation.
LiLi searches INLINEFORM1, INLINEFORM2, INLINEFORM3 in INLINEFORM4, sets bits in INLINEFORM5, randomly sets INLINEFORM14 with probability INLINEFORM15, and updates KS with triple INLINEFORM18.
LiLi asks the user for a clue (+ve instance) for INLINEFORM1 and corrupts INLINEFORM2 and INLINEFORM3 to generate -ve instances for training the prediction model for INLINEFORM5.

If LiLi wins the episode, it adds INLINEFORM1 to data buffers INLINEFORM2 based on mode INLINEFORM3, populates validation buffer INLINEFORM8 and evaluation buffer INLINEFORM9, or invokes the prediction model for INLINEFORM11.

For Lifelong Relation Prediction, LiLi trains a prediction model using INLINEFORM1 and INLINEFORM2, takes 10% of instances from INLINEFORM10, uses a LSTM BIBREF40, computes INLINEFORM16, maximizes log-likelihood of INLINEFORM19, updates INLINEFORM21, trains an inverse model, and uses relation-specific prediction threshold INLINEFORM29.

Parameter settings for LiLi include empirically set parameters in Table 1, INLINEFORM11-greedy strategy, pre-training steps=50000, Keras, batch-size 128, max. training epoch 150, dropout 0.2, hidden units and embedding size 300, learning rate 5e-3, factor 0.5, patience 5, Adam optimizer, early stopping, shuffling INLINEFORM14, and class weights adjusted inversely proportional to class frequencies in INLINEFORM15.

For relation INLINEFORM0 and observed triple (INLINEFORM1, INLINEFORM2, INLINEFORM3), pair (INLINEFORM4, INLINEFORM5) is a +ve instance, and two negative ones are generated by corrupting source INLINEFORM9 and target INLINEFORM10.
Single is the version of LiLi where a single prediction model INLINEFORM0 is trained for all test relations.
Sep does not transfer past learned weights for initializing INLINEFORM0, disabling LL.
F-th) uses a fixed prediction threshold 0.5 instead of relation-specific threshold INLINEFORM0.
Evaluation Metrics introduce Coverage(INLINEFORM0), where INLINEFORM1 is 1.0 if LiLi wins all episodes, and use Avg. MCC and avg. +ve F1 score for predictive performance.
